## Overview

The Taungyo (Burmese: *တောင်ရိုး လူမျိုး* Tauñyoù lumyoù) are a sub-ethnic group of the Bamar people. They live primarily in Shan State and are centered on Pindaya. The sources describe Taungyo as speaking Taungyo (*တောင်ရိုးစကား* Tauñyoùs̱áḵà), characterized as a Tavoyan dialect of Burmese. Taungyo has 89% lexical similarity with standard Burmese and is closely related to Danu, Intha and Rakhine. The available sources contain no population figure for the Taungyo and do not describe their material culture, artistic traditions, religious practices, or social institutions.

## Language & religion

Taungyo is described as a dialect of Burmese, and Taungyo is also described as closely related to Danu, Intha and Rakhine. The sources state that Taungyo has 89% lexical similarity with standard Burmese. The listed Taungyo vocabulary includes *anak* for “red,” *amrang* for “high,” *myak-sai* for “eye,” and *lang* for “light.”

The related description of Tavoyan or Dawei identifies it as a divergent dialect of Burmese spoken in Dawei (Tavoy), in the coastal Tanintharyi Region of southern Myanmar (Burma). Tavoyan speakers self-identify as Bamar and are classified by the Burmese government as a subgroup of the Bamar. The sources give no account of Taungyo religious affiliation or spiritual practices.

The Tavoyan description states that approximately 400,000 people speak Tavoyan and that Tavoyan and Burmese have 87% lexical similarity. It describes differences in prosody, vowels, consonant voicing, medial consonants, nasalisation, phonemes, and vocabulary. Tavoyan retains an /-l-/ medial that merged into the /-j-/ medial in standard Burmese, and it has loan words from Malay and Thai. According to Michael Aung-Thwin, the dialect preserved the “spelling (and presumably pronunciation)” of Old Burmese from the Bagan era. The source places its divergence from other Burmese varieties sometime after Burmese settlement of Lower Burma under the Bagan era, between the 11th and 13th centuries, and states that the Bamar are called *gantha* (*ဂံသား*, “children of Pagan”) in Tavoyan.
